name: You Didn't Choose The Image; It's Deciding For You
description: Join us for a lecture that asks a deceptively simple question: who actually gets to decide what a hero, a victim, or a good life looks like?About the LectureWe don't choose the images that come to define us, and yet they decide more than we realise. A single gaze on a movie poster decides who counts as a hero. A familiar narrative arc decides who counts as a believable victim. A curated feed decides what a good life is supposed to look like.This talk moves through three of the speaker's own published studies — on Malayalam movie poster semiotics, on how Bollywood narratives construct the "ideal" rape victim, and on Instagram, loneliness, and FoMO among young Indians — to trace one quiet mechanism running underneath very different parts of Indian media. By the end, the question isn't really about posters, films, or apps. It's about who gets to build the image in the first place, and what we do with the gap between it and our own lives.About the SpeakerLydia Glory Jose is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Media and Journalism at IILM University, Gurugram, where she teaches media studies, visual communication, and research methods. Before academia, she worked as a journalist with Malayala Manorama, an experience that continues to shape how she reads Indian media — from the inside, not as an outsider looking in. Her research sits at the intersection of representation, visual semiotics, and digital media, published in Springer Nature's Sexuality and Culture, Palabra Clave, and the International Journal of Semiotics and Visual Rhetoric, and cited by the Times of India. Multilingual in Malayalam, Hindi, English, and Arabic, she remains, at heart, more interested in what an image is doing to us than in what it appears to be showing us.PS: Your Ticket Includes a 250/- Coupon Redeemable on F&BAbout unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from St. Stephen's, Delhi who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive. Each event is an invitation to spend an evening with an idea.

name: uL: Badass Begums, The Women Of The Mughal Era
description: Join us for a lecture that steps into a side of Delhi's history that rarely makes it into textbooks: The women who built this city.About the LectureWhen we think of Mughal Delhi, we think of emperors. We think of conquest, succession, and the men whose names are carved into monuments. But behind — and often alongside — those names were formidable women whose influence shaped the city through architecture, politics, philanthropy, and patronage.They commissioned buildings. They brokered power. They funded entire neighbourhoods. And then, almost entirely, they were written out of the story.Drawing on rare paintings, forgotten anecdotes, and lesser-known archival stories, historian and author Anoushka Jain brings these women back into the history of the city they helped create.The session explores:Who the Mughal women behind Delhi's architecture and politics really wereHow begums and princesses wielded influence through patronage, charity, and urban designThe stories and images that have been overlooked or erased from mainstream historical narrativesWhat these legacies reveal about women, power, and public life in Mughal IndiaAbout the SpeakerAnoushka Jain is a historian, author, and founder of Enroute Indian History, a heritage initiative dedicated to uncovering and sharing India's lesser-known histories. She is the author of Badass Begums (HarperCollins India), a book that explores the lives of remarkable women who shaped the cultural and political landscape of Delhi.Her work has appeared in The Hindu, The Indian Express, Scroll.in, The Print, Hindustan Times, The Times of India, and Vogue India.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive. unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: What's Your Move? Decision-Making Ideas from ‘Go'
description: Join us for a lecture — and a game — that starts with a question you face 35,000 times a day:What's your move?About the LectureHow do we make choices? Not the easy ones — tea or coffee, left or right — but the ones that shape careers, relationships, and the texture of a life. Most of us were never taught how to decide. We improvise. We copy. We freeze. And then we wonder why things turned out the way they did.There's a game that has been teaching people how to think about exactly this — for four thousand years.Go — known as Baduk in Korea and Weiqi in China — is the oldest continuously played strategy game in the world. Its rules are breathtakingly simple. Its possibilities outnumber the atoms in the universe. Buddhist monks played it as a practice in mindfulness. Military strategists studied it for its lessons in territory and timing. And at its heart, every single move is a decision — one that cannot be taken back.Pieces once placed are not moved. You live with your choices. You watch how a decision in one corner of the board ripples into another. You learn to see connections, anticipate consequences, and hold the whole picture in your mind while acting on the smallest part of it.This lecture draws on the ancient wisdom of Go — and on professional players' strategies — to explore timeless ideas about how we make decisions and how we might make better ones.The session explores:Why most of us struggle with decision-making — and what we were never taughtHow Go models the real-life dynamics of choice: you, other players, and the environment you shareThe importance of detachment, vision, and reading the situation before you actWhat professional Go strategies reveal about creativity, patience, and riskHow a 4,000-year-old board game can sharpen the way you navigate modern lifeWe'll start by learning Go and playing a game together — because the best way to understand decisions is to make a few.About the SpeakerPrabhat Prakash is the Founder of Go Higher Ventures, an enterprise for Decision Education. He has delivered unique programs leveraging the strategy game Go to teach decision-making concepts to students from reputed public schools. He is the author of What's Your Move? 9 Timeless Ideas for Making Decisions (releasing soon), and is an experienced Go player with a 5k all-time high rank. He has worked across the Higher Education, International Development, and Banking sectors, and is a management graduate from St. Xavier's College, Mumbai.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive. unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

I started curating these experiences to make age-old crafts more accessible to the art-curious while creating meaningful opportunities for master artisans to share their knowledge. I believe cultural heritage thrives when it's experienced. Through intimate workshops, I hope to build a community that celebrates traditional arts, supports artisan livelihoods, and carries these legacies forward together.

name: Humayun's Tomb : Heritage Walk
description: About the ExperienceExplore the Humayun's Tomb complex on a guided heritage walk and learn about its history, architecture, and cultural significance. Built in the 16th century by Haji Begum in memory of Emperor Humayun, the monument is one of the earliest examples of Mughal garden tomb architecture in India.The walk covers the main mausoleum along with other important monuments within the complex, including Isa Khan's Tomb, Arab Sarai, Barber's Tomb, the mosque, and Afsarwala's Tomb. Throughout the experience, the storyteller will share historical context, architectural features, and interesting facts about the site.The walk is conducted at a comfortable pace and includes opportunities for questions and photography.

name: In Search Of Djinns : Kotla Feroz Shah Walk
description: The walk takes you inside the fort of the 14th century ruler Firoz Shah Tughlaq built for his new capital Firozabad. The Kushak-e- Firoz (the Palace of Firoz) was strategically built at the banks of River Yamuna. The fort faced riverfront and lush green plains, its staircase leading you to the banks. It has a functioning mosque, a circular baoli (stepwell) known to have water snakes and a hypnotic effect on its visitors (it has recently been barricaded). The fort also has the magnificent Ashokan Pillar in Pali text erected at a height. It is confounding to any visitor how almost 27 tonne of heavy weighing monolith pillar was taken from Haryana and planted inside the fort at such a great height!Every Thursday evening Djinn (supernatural creatures in Islamic mythology) worship is performed in the complex, with visitors leaving their wish list, and a thread tied to the lattice for the Djinns to fulfill their wishes! The fort in recent years has gained the reputation of being haunted, because of the strong belief of Djinns inhabiting the fort.

name: Safdarjung Tomb Night Heritage Walk
description: Safdarjung’s Tomb Heritage Walkcurated by Darwesh heritage walks in collaboration with Sabhyata Foundation.Join us for a journey into the fading glow of Mughal splendour at Safdarjung's Tomb — often called the *last flicker of Mughal grandeur* in Delhi.Built in 1754 for Safdarjung, the powerful Nawab of Awadh and Prime Minister of the Mughal court, this monument stands at the twilight of an empire — grand in ambition, yet carrying within it the quiet signs of decline.Its story is as fascinating as its form. From courtly intrigues and shifting loyalties to the architectural choices that reveal a changing political landscape, Safdarjung’s life opens a compelling window into 18th-century Delhi.We will also trace a lesser-known layer of its history — how this tomb was constructed by reusing material from a pre-existing Mughal structure, quite literally building one memory over another.To truly understand Delhi — its rise, its resilience, and its gradual transitions — a visit to Safdarjung’s Tomb is essential.Come, walk with us through the final chapter of Mughal architectural brilliance — where grandeur meets gravity, and history lingers in every arch.

name: National Museum (Indus Valley Civilisation)
description: Step into the fascinating world of the Indus Valley Civilization at the iconic National Museum and uncover the mysteries of one of the world’s oldest urban cultures. From advanced city planning and drainage systems to intricate seals, jewellery, pottery, and trade networks, this walk takes you deep into the lives of a civilization that flourished over 4,500 years ago.Explore the stories hidden behind ancient artefacts, decode symbols that still remain unsolved, and discover how the people of Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro were far ahead of their time. Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a curious explorer, or someone who simply loves untold stories, this immersive museum experience promises a journey through India’s remarkable ancient past.Join us as history comes alive — one artefact, one mystery, and one story at a time.

description: The August screening brings you a cinematically brilliant film, The Giants.Synopsis:The Giants portrays the deep connection between trees and humans through the life of Australian environmental hero and the Australian parliament’s first openly gay member, Bob Brown.
